vignette:
Kwame was 27 when the war reached his village in the eastern highlands. He had been a teacher then, not a soldier, but when the militia came through he fled into the forest with a dozen others. For three days they moved at night, hiding in thickets by day. On the fourth morning a mortar round hit their camp. The flames swept through the dry brush and eight people died—some burned, some shot as they ran. Kwame survived because he had been gathering water farther down the slope, and when he returned the fire was still crackling and the bodies were unrecognizable. He had hidden behind a boulder and done nothing. That was the moment he first felt the weight of what he had not done, and it has never left him.

Kwame emigrated to the United States in his thirties and became a park ranger in a sprawling national forest. The work seemed to offer solitude, but it has instead become a daily confrontation. Every time he patrols a trail that winds through tall pines, the smell of dry bark and the sound of wind in the leaves pull him back to that hillside, and he feels the old guilt rising. Being in nature, especially in open terrain with underbrush, is a direct route to the memory of bodies and flames. He can feel his pulse quicken; his chest tightens and he starts scanning the tree line for threats. When a visitor corrects him about a trail closure or a supervisor offers a suggestion on his report, the criticism lands like an accusation. He hears it as a judgment: you should have done more, you failed then and you are failing now. The guilt intensifies, and with it the belief that he is fundamentally different from the people around him—isolated, set apart, someone who acted in ways that violate his own values. He had survived by staying hidden, and he cannot forgive himself for that. This conviction that he was, at root, a coward made him scan the forest for any echo of that judgment—the crack of a twig, the smell of burnt pine, the shape of a person moving through the brush—until the ordinary landscape itself became a minefield of reminders.

Over the months, Kwame’s sense of threat has become pervasive. He cannot relax even in his own cabin, which he knows is safe; a door clicking shut or a car backfiring on the access road sends a jolt through him. He lies awake for hours, replaying the crack of the mortar and the shouts in a language he barely understood. Delays—a shipment of supplies not arriving on time, a ranger meeting starting late—feel like the first sign of something terrible brewing. The more he expects danger, the more he notices potential triggers. A vehicle with dark-tinted windows, a visitor wearing a camouflage jacket, the glint of sunlight on a metal hiking pole—each becomes a cue that jolts him back to the war zone. He has come to believe that the safest response is to cut himself off entirely. He stopped answering calls from his sister two years ago. He avoids the ranger station whenever possible, especially if anyone is wearing a uniform or carrying a firearm; the sight of a sidearm on a colleague’s hip makes his mouth go dry and his legs feel weak. But every detour he took to sidestep the station became its own encounter with the memory—the longer route through the back trails, the careful timing of his arrivals, each reroute a fresh reminder of what he was avoiding and why. Instead he drinks beer alone in his cabin most evenings, enough to blur the edges of his vigilance. But the alcohol also worsens his sleep, leaving him groggy and more vulnerable to the next day’s threats.

The loop tightens. When he encounters a trigger—say, a patch of scorched earth after a controlled burn—the guilt surges, and that guilt itself makes him more watchful for further signs of danger, more convinced that something bad is about to happen. The heightened threat in turn drives him to drink more and to isolate further. And every time he cancels a plan or walks away from a conversation, the isolation confirms what he already believes: that he does not belong among ordinary people, that he is and always will be the man who hid. He has not been on a social outing in more than a year. The one time he drove into town for groceries, a man in a delivery uniform approached him with a clipboard, and Kwame abandoned his cart and fled.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a night last week when he could not sleep at all. He had seen a documentary playing in the break room—a few seconds of news footage from a different conflict—and the flames had returned to his dreams. He woke at 3 a.m., convinced he smelled smoke, and spent an hour checking the cabin’s outlets and stove. The next morning he called a number for employee assistance, his hand shaking. He is afraid that if he does not find a way out, he will lose this job too, and then there will be nothing left. He is most afraid of the silence he has created around himself—and of what he might do if the guilt becomes unbearable. Feeling this perpetually unsafe had, over the months, quietly hardened into proof that he was no longer a man who deserved to feel at ease—that the world had marked him as someone who could not be trusted, least of all by himself.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, self-blame) cause the patient to experience triggers; instead, triggers lead to guilt and guilt leads to threat, not directly to triggers.

The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes negative appraisals; threat leads to maladaptive strategies and maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals, but threat→negative appraisals is missing.
The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, drinking) cause the patient to encounter triggers; triggers lead to maladaptive strategies, not the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, self-blame) cause the patient to experience triggers; instead, triggers lead to guilt and guilt leads to threat, not directly to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes negative appraisals; threat leads to maladaptive strategies and maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals, but threat→negative appraisals is missing.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, drinking) cause the patient to encounter triggers; triggers lead to maladaptive strategies, not the reverse.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
